newsitem.title: IRAQ: Oil deal supplies to pour into Iraq by end of month.
newsitem.headline: Oil deal supplies to pour into Iraq by end of month.

text.p: Shipments of food and medical supplies under Iraq's oil deal with the United Nations are expected to flow into the country by the end of February, diplomats in Baghdad said on Sunday.

They said money from Iraq's partial oil sales was accumulating in an escrow account in New York and the United Nations was expected to be able to pay during this month for the deployment of observers and purchases of wheat, sugar, rice and other essential commodities.
"A couple of food observers have already arrived. More are expected in coming weeks which means that the U.N. has finally got some of the oil money," one diplomat said.

A U.N. spokesman said on Thursday money paid into an escrow account holding proceeds from the sale of Iraqi oil would total $239 million by the end of the day, when a deposit of $23.4 million was expected.

The account was opened under an oil-for-food deal that became effective on December 10. It enables Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies to help offset the effects of sanctions imposed on Iraq since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The U.N. needs to position about 151 international observers in Iraq before stocks of supplies from the partial oil sales are built up and then handed out to Iraqis.
Iraq's oil hit the international markets on December 12 and diplomats said barring unforseen difficulties Iraqis should be able to get their new food rations from the oil money by the end of March.

Iraq was said to have signed contracts to buy wheat from both France and Australia. Traders in Baghdad said contracts for the purchase of rice, sugar and other commodities from France, Thailand and Turkey were also signed.
But diplomats said no money for any of the contracts was yet paid from Iraq's escrow account. Iraq has earmarked about $805 million of its oil money for food supplies and $210 million for medicine.
It needs 1.3 million tonnes of wheat flour, 319,000 tonnes of rice and 256,00 tonnes of sugar to meet needs covering six months.
One diplomat said Iraqi and U.N. officials were busy trying to remove last hurdles on the duties of U.N. observers.
"I believe they still need to solve issues concerning their freedom of movement, logistics and what type of communications gear they are to use," he said.

He said the costs of accommodating the observers and paying for their other expenses were adding up. He did not say exactly how much Iraq would need to pay to meet their needs but he said the cost could eventually run into millions of dollars.
"They (observers) need support staff, vehicles, computers, lodging and accomodation and latest communications equipment," the diplomat said.
But he said Iraq was still keen to let the deal go through as it believed the flow of supplies on such a large-scale would ease the impact of the U.N. embargo.

More than $1.3 billion from the partial oil sales will enter Iraq's economy in the form of food and medicine in six months, relieving the government of the burden of paying about $100 million each month to subsidise the current food rations.
